summary: Specifies the conventions for using the US Government's NSA Suite B cryptography in IPsec. Because many Suite B algorithms are used elsewhere, most conventions are already given in other documents, so this profile mostly references those. It is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6380 turns the NSA's Suite B algorithm policy into rules for IPsec. It fixes which encryption, signing, key exchange and hashing algorithms may be used, and adds two levels of strength: a 128-bit level and a stronger 192-bit one that allows only the larger sizes.

subtitle: The rules for using the NSA's Suite B algorithms inside IPsec, including which curves and key sizes go with which security level.

tldr.problem: IPsec lets an organisation choose from many algorithms, so a national security deployment needs a fixed policy rather than a free choice.
tldr.mechanism: Suite B fixes the algorithm set: AES encryption, ECDSA signatures and ECDH key exchange on the P-256 and P-384 curves, and SHA-256 or SHA-384 hashing, with two security levels that decide which sizes are allowed and which of the four named cipher suites may be offered.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is mostly a pointer to where each convention is already written down, with the details repeated where a developer needs them. It is an Informational document and is Historic today.

facts.label: Key exchange group
facts.value: 256-bit or 384-bit random ECP group, Transform Type 4

facts.label: SKEYSEED, SK_d, SK_pi and SK_pr
facts.value: 256 bits with PRF-HMAC-SHA-256, 384 bits with PRF-HMAC-SHA-384

today: RFC 6380 is Historic, so it is no longer a current standards document, and the unit metadata lists no replacement RFC for it. It was published in October 2011 as an Informational document setting out the conventions for using NSA Suite B cryptography in IPsec, and it says that because many of the Suite B algorithms are used elsewhere, most of those conventions are already specified in other documents.

sections.title: What Suite B Is and What This Document Adds
sections.content:
The United States Government published guidelines for NSA Suite B Cryptography in July 2005, defining cryptographic algorithm policy for national security applications. RFC 6380 specifies the conventions for using Suite B cryptography in IP Security.

IPsec provides confidentiality, data integrity, access control and data source authentication for IP datagrams. The Internet Key Exchange provides automated key management for IPsec, performing mutual authentication between two parties and establishing security associations that protect both the IKE conversation and the IPsec traffic itself. A Suite B compliant IPsec implementation MUST use IKEv2.

RFC 6379 defines four cryptographic user interface suites for IPsec built from Suite B algorithms. They give options for IKEv2 and for the IP Encapsulating Security Payload, ESP. A Suite B compliant IPsec implementation MUST use one of those four suites, chosen according to the desired security level and the security services wanted.

The document is deliberately thin. Because many of the Suite B algorithms are used in other environments, most of the conventions needed are already specified elsewhere; this RFC references the source of those conventions and repeats some relevant detail to help developers who choose to support Suite B.
sections.plainLanguage: IPsec offers a menu of algorithms, and Suite B is a way of narrowing that menu to a fixed list published by the National Security Agency. This RFC says which entries are allowed at which strength, and points at the other documents that already explain how each one works.

sections.title: The Suite B Algorithms
sections.content:
Suite B requires that key establishment and signature algorithms be based on elliptic curve cryptography, and that the encryption algorithm be AES. The set is:

  • Encryption: the Advanced Encryption Standard, with key sizes of 128 and 256 bits.
  • Digital signature: the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm, ECDSA, using the curves with 256-bit and 384-bit prime moduli.
  • Key exchange: Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman, ECDH, using the curves with 256-bit and 384-bit prime moduli.
  • Hashes: SHA-256 and SHA-384.

The two elliptic curves appear in the literature under two different names, so the RFC lists both along with the Diffie-Hellman group numbers IANA has assigned. The 256-bit curve is P-256, called nistp256 by NIST and secp256r1 by the SECG, and is group 19. The 384-bit curve is P-384, called nistp384 by NIST and secp384r1 by the SECG, and is group 20. IANA has already registered both groups.
sections.plainLanguage: Suite B pairs the AES block cipher with elliptic curve cryptography for signing and for agreeing a shared key, and with the two SHA-2 hash functions. Two curves are named, one 256-bit and one 384-bit, and each has a NIST name, a SECG name and an assigned group number.

sections.title: Security Levels and Allowed Suites
sections.content:
Suite B provides two levels of cryptographic security: a 128-bit minimum level of security, called minLOS_128, and a 192-bit minimum level, minLOS_192. Each level defines a minimum strength that all the cryptographic algorithms must provide.

The non-signature primitives fall into two columns. Column 1 holds AES-128 for encryption, ECDH on P-256 for key agreement and SHA256 for the pseudorandom function and the MAC. Column 2 holds AES-256, ECDH on P-384 and SHA384. At the 128-bit level the non-signature primitives MUST come exclusively from Column 1 or exclusively from Column 2. At the 192-bit level they MUST come exclusively from Column 2.

Each system MUST specify a security level of at least 128 bits or 192 bits, and that level decides which of the four suites from RFC 6379 are allowed. The four are Suite-B-GCM-128, Suite-B-GMAC-128, Suite-B-GCM-256 and Suite-B-GMAC-256, and they satisfy the Suite B requirements.

At the 128-bit level one of the four MUST be used. At the 192-bit level only two are permitted: Suite-B-GCM-256 or Suite-B-GMAC-256, and one of those MUST be used.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two strength settings. The lower one allows either the smaller or the larger algorithms, but not a mixture of the two columns. The higher one allows only the larger algorithms. The suite names tell you which key size and which mode of operation each option uses.

sections.title: Authentication and Certificates
sections.content:
Digital signatures using ECDSA MUST be used for authentication by Suite B compliant implementations. RFC 4754 defines two such algorithms: ECDSA-256, which is ECDSA on the P-256 curve with the SHA-256 hash function, and ECDSA-384, which is ECDSA on the P-384 curve with SHA-384.

At the 128-bit level a system MUST use either ECDSA-256 or ECDSA-384 for IKE authentication, and it is allowable for one party to authenticate with ECDSA-256 while the other uses ECDSA-384, so that an initiator and a responder with different key sizes can still interoperate. Initiators and responders at that level MUST be able to verify ECDSA-256 signatures and SHOULD be able to verify ECDSA-384 signatures. At the 192-bit level ECDSA-384 MUST be used by both parties, and both MUST be able to verify ECDSA-384 signatures.

Authentication methods other than ECDSA-256 and ECDSA-384 MUST NOT be used for IKEv2 authentication. If a relying party receives a message signed with any other authentication method it MUST return an AUTHENTICATION_FAILED notification and stop processing the message.

At both levels the initiator and the responder MUST each use an X.509 certificate that complies with the Suite B Certificate and Certificate Revocation List profile of RFC 5759, and that contains an elliptic curve public key with the key usage bit set for digital signature.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides prove who they are with a signature made on an elliptic curve key, and both sides must accept a certificate that follows the Suite B certificate profile. At the stronger level only the larger curve is allowed, and a message signed any other way must be rejected outright.

sections.title: Negotiating Suites and Deriving Keys
sections.content:
The four suites differ in algorithm strength and in whether ESP provides confidentiality and integrity together or integrity alone. The names give the AES mode, GCM or GMAC, and the AES key length, 128 or 256. Suites with GCM in their name MUST be used when ESP integrity protection and encryption are both needed. Suites with GMAC in their name MUST be used only when there is no need for ESP encryption.

An initiator at the 128-bit level MUST offer one or more of the four suites, and if it offers Suite-B-GCM-128 or Suite-B-GMAC-128 those MUST appear in the IKEv2 and IPsec SA payloads before any offering of the 256-bit suites. A responder at that level MUST support one or both of the two 128-bit suites and SHOULD support one or both of the two 256-bit suites, and it MUST accept one of the Suite B suites. If none of the four are offered it MUST return a Notify payload with the error NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN when operating in Suite B compliant mode. At the 192-bit level the initiator MUST offer one or both of the two 256-bit suites and the responder MUST choose one of them, returning NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN if neither is offered.

Both sides MUST generate an ephemeral elliptic curve key pair for the ECDH key exchange, on P-256 when the 256-bit random ECP group for Transform Type 4 is selected and on P-384 when the 384-bit group is selected. The ephemeral public keys MUST be stored in the key exchange payload as in RFC 5903. The shared secret is the x value of the ECDH common value, 256 or 384 bits wide. The RFC also carries over the rule from NIST SP800-56A that an ephemeral private key must be used in exactly one key establishment transaction and must be zeroized after use, and that the shared secret must be zeroized immediately after its use.

The derived key material has fixed sizes. With PRF-HMAC-SHA-256, SKEYSEED, SK_d, SK_pi and SK_pr MUST each be 256 bits; with PRF-HMAC-SHA-384, each 384 bits. SK_ai and SK_ar MUST be 256 or 384 bits when HMAC-SHA-256-128 or HMAC-SHA-384-192 is used, and SK_ei and SK_er MUST be 128 or 256 bits when the key length attribute for AES_ENC_CBC is set to 128 or 256.

There are further rules about what the protocol may negotiate. AH is not supported in Suite B compliant implementations. A Diffie-Hellman group MAY be negotiated for a Child SA, and where a Transform Type 4 is specified for an ESP SA its value MUST match that used by the IKE SA. A KEi payload in a CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange MUST use the same random ECP group as the IKE_SA_INIT exchange, and rekeying of the CREATE_CHILD_SA MUST be supported by both parties, with any Diffie-Hellman key using that same group. A compliant system MUST support IKEv2 and MUST NOT use IKEv1 between a compliant initiator and responder; it may be configured to use IKEv1 as long as only IKEv2 is used between such peers, but then it is not operating in a Suite B compliant mode. The IKEv2 authentication method MUST NOT use the Identification Payloads for policy lookup, and must instead use an end entity found in the certificate the authenticating party supplied. The administrative interface MUST let the operator pick a single suite, and may let the operator pick several with a preferred order following Section 4.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides agree on one of the four named suites, generate a temporary key on the agreed curve to agree a shared secret, and derive the traffic keys from it. The rules pin down exactly which suite may be offered, in what order, and what happens if nothing matches.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it discusses security requirements throughout, and that it inherits the security considerations of RFC 4303 on ESP, RFC 4754 on ECDSA authentication, RFC 5759 on the Suite B certificate profile and RFC 5996 on IKEv2. The security rules of the document itself are the ones stated throughout: the algorithm set, the two security levels, the exclusive-column rule, the signature algorithms that are allowed, the certificate profile that must be used, the fixed key sizes and the rules on ephemeral keys and their zeroization.
sections.plainLanguage: The document's security content is in the rules themselves, spread through its sections, and it leans on four other documents for the background on ESP, elliptic curve signatures, certificates and key exchange.

viz.caption: THE FOUR FAMILIES OF ALGORITHM IN SUITE B

items.title: Encryption
items.text: AES, with key sizes of 128 and 256 bits.

items.title: Digital signature
items.text: ECDSA, on the curves with 256-bit and 384-bit prime moduli.

items.title: Key exchange
items.text: Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman, on the same two curves.

viz.caption: THE TWO COLUMNS OF NON-SIGNATURE PRIMITIVES
THE FOUR SUITE B USER INTERFACE SUITES

items.label: GCM, 128-bit key
items.desc: Encrypts and protects the integrity of the traffic, with a 128-bit AES key.

items.label: GMAC, 128-bit key
items.desc: Protects the integrity of the traffic only, with a 128-bit AES key. Used when there is no need for encryption.

items.label: GCM, 256-bit key
items.desc: Encrypts and protects the integrity of the traffic, with a 256-bit AES key.

items.label: GMAC, 256-bit key
items.desc: Protects the integrity of the traffic only, with a 256-bit AES key. Used when there is no need for encryption.
